question_description: Given an array of integers and a target sum, find if there exists a pair of elements in the array that sum up to the target value. Return true if such a pair exists, false otherwise. Example: Input: [1, 4, 45, 6, 10, 8], target = 16. Output: true (6 + 10 = 16)
question_answers: Use nested loops to check all possible pairs. For each element, iterate through the rest of the array to find if any other element sums to the target. This approach has O(n²) time complexity and O(1) space complexity.

Sort the array first, then use two pointers - one at the beginning and one at the end. Move pointers inward based on whether the current sum is less than or greater than the target. This approach has O(n log n) time complexity due to sorting.

Use a hash set to store visited elements. For each element, check if (target - current) exists in the set. If found, return true; otherwise add current element to set. This approach has O(n) time complexity and O(n) space complexity.

Use binary search for each element after sorting. For each element, search for (target - element) in the sorted array using binary search. This approach has O(n log n) time complexity due to sorting and binary searches.
question_hint: Think about using a data structure that allows O(1) lookups to check if the complement (target - current) has been seen before.

question_name: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
question_description:
Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i-th day, find the maximum profit you can achieve by buying on one day and selling on a later day. If no profit can be achieved, return 0.

Example: prices = [7,1,5,3,6,4] → Output: 5 (buy at day 2 (price=1) and sell at day 5 (price=6))
question_answers: Use nested loops to check every possible buy-sell pair. For each day i as buy day, iterate through all subsequent days j as sell day, calculate profit = prices[j] - prices[i], and track maximum profit. Time complexity O(n²).

Track minimum price seen so far while iterating through array. For each price, calculate potential profit if selling at current price after buying at minimum price. Update maximum profit and minimum price as you go. Time complexity O(n).

Use dynamic programming with two states: holding stock and not holding stock. For each day, track maximum profit in each state. This approach can handle multiple transactions but is overkill for single transaction. Time complexity O(n).

Sort the array and find maximum difference between elements, but this doesn't respect chronological order. This approach fails because it doesn't maintain the buy-before-sell constraint. Time complexity O(n log n).
Use prefix minimums array to track minimum price up to each day. Then for each day, calculate profit as current price minus prefix minimum. Track maximum profit. Time complexity O(n) with O(n) space.
question_hint: Think about tracking the minimum price seen so far as you iterate through the array.

question_description: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and without using the division operation. Example: Input: nums = [1,2,3,4] Output: [24,12,8,6]
question_answers: Use nested loops to calculate product for each element by multiplying all other elements, resulting in O(n²) time complexity with O(1) extra space.
Calculate total product of all elements first, then for each element divide total product by current element, but this violates the 'no division' constraint and has issues with zeros.
Use prefix and suffix products arrays - compute left products first, then right products, and combine them to get result in O(n) time with O(n) space.
Use a single output array with two passes - first pass computes left products, second pass multiplies with right products using a running variable, achieving O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
question_hint: Think about computing products from left to right and right to left separately, then combine them efficiently.

question_description: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray (containing at least one number) which has the largest sum and return its sum. Example: Input: nums = [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4], Output: 6, Explanation: [4,-1,2,1] has the largest sum = 6.
question_answers: Use nested loops to check all possible subarrays, calculate each sum, and track the maximum. This brute force approach has O(n²) time complexity.
Use a divide and conquer approach similar to merge sort, recursively finding maximum subarray in left, right, and crossing subarrays. This has O(n log n) time complexity.
Use Kadane's algorithm with dynamic programming, maintaining current sum and maximum sum while iterating through the array. This has O(n) time complexity and O(1) space.
Use prefix sums with a min prefix tracker, calculating maximum subarray sum as current prefix minus minimum prefix seen so far. This has O(n) time complexity.
question_hint: Think about tracking both current subarray sum and maximum sum found so far while iterating through the array.

question_description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, find the maximum amount of water that can be trapped between two bars. For example, given heights = [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7], the maximum water area is 49.
question_answers: Use nested loops to check all possible pairs of bars, calculate area for each pair using min(height[i], height[j]) * (j-i), and keep track of maximum area found.
Sort the heights with their indices, then use two pointers from the sorted array to find maximum area while maintaining original positions.
Use a stack-based approach to find next greater elements in both directions, then calculate water trapped between each bar and its boundaries.
Use two pointers starting at both ends, calculate area with current pointers, then move the pointer with smaller height inward, repeating until pointers meet.
Use dynamic programming to precompute left and right maximum heights for each position, then calculate water at each bar and sum for total area.
question_hint: Think about how the area is limited by the shorter bar and the distance between bars. Can you find a way to avoid checking all pairs?

question_description: Calculate factorial of a large number (n ≤ 1000) and return the result as a string. For example, factorial(5) = "120", factorial(10) = "3628800". The result can be very large, so it cannot be stored in standard integer types.
question_answers: Use recursion to calculate factorial directly, but this will fail for large numbers due to integer overflow and recursion depth limits.
Use a loop with double or long double to handle larger numbers, but this still has precision limitations for very large factorials.
Use Python's built-in big integers or Java's BigInteger class which can handle arbitrarily large numbers natively.
Implement manual multiplication using arrays or strings to store each digit, multiplying step by step like elementary school multiplication.
Use a linked list to store digits and perform multiplication, keeping track of carries at each digit position during multiplication.
Use an array to store digits in reverse order, multiply the current result by each number from 2 to n, handling carries properly at each step.
question_hint: Think about how you would multiply large numbers by hand - store digits in an array and handle carries.

question_description: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining. Example: Input: height = [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1], Output: 6
question_answers: Use two pointers approach scanning from both ends, tracking max heights on left and right. Water at each position is determined by the minimum of left and right max heights minus current height. This runs in O(n) time with O(1) space.

Create left and right max arrays by scanning twice. For each position, water trapped is min(leftMax[i], rightMax[i]) - height[i]. This approach uses O(n) time and O(n) space but is straightforward to understand.
Brute force approach: For each position, find maximum height to left and right by scanning entire array. Water trapped is min(leftMax, rightMax) - height[i]. This takes O(n²) time and O(1) space.
Use a stack to track decreasing heights. When a higher bar is found, pop from stack and calculate water between current bar and previous bar in stack. This approach uses O(n) time and O(n) space.
Sort the heights and use mathematical formula to calculate trapped water based on sorted order. This approach takes O(n log n) time and O(n) space but is less intuitive for this problem.
question_hint: Think about how water at each position is limited by the minimum of the maximum heights on its left and right sides.

question_description: Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by their start time, and a new interval to insert, insert the new interval into the list and merge any overlapping intervals. Return the list of intervals after insertion and merging. Example: intervals = [[1,3],[6,9]], newInterval = [2,5] → [[1,5],[6,9]]
question_answers: Create a new list and iterate through intervals, adding non-overlapping intervals before the new one. When encountering overlap, merge by updating the new interval's start and end. Finally add remaining intervals after the merged one.

First add the new interval to the list, then sort all intervals by start time. Iterate through sorted intervals, merging overlapping ones by comparing current interval's start with previous interval's end.

Use binary search to find insertion position for the new interval. Then iterate left and right to merge overlapping intervals, updating boundaries as needed. This avoids unnecessary sorting of all intervals.
Create three lists: intervals before new interval, overlapping intervals to merge, and intervals after. Merge overlapping intervals by taking min start and max end, then combine all three lists.

Iterate through intervals while tracking a result list. For each interval, if it doesn't overlap with new interval, add it. If overlap occurs, merge by expanding new interval boundaries. Add merged interval at appropriate position.
question_hint: Since intervals are already sorted, you can take advantage of this property to avoid sorting the entire list again.

question_description: Given a collection of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals. For example, given intervals [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]], return [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]].
question_answers: Sort intervals by start time, then iterate through them. For each interval, if it overlaps with the previous merged interval, merge them by updating the end time. Otherwise, add it as a new interval.
Use a brute force approach: for each interval, compare it with all other intervals to find overlaps and merge them. This requires nested loops and repeated comparisons.

First sort intervals by start time. Then use a stack to track merged intervals. Push first interval, then for each subsequent interval, if it overlaps with top of stack, merge by updating end time, else push it.
Use a hash map to track all covered points, then reconstruct intervals from the covered ranges. This approach marks all points covered by intervals and then finds contiguous ranges.
Sort intervals by start time, then use a two-pointer approach. Keep track of current merged interval and update its end when overlapping intervals are found. Add to result when no more overlaps.
question_hint: Think about sorting the intervals first to make overlapping intervals adjacent to each other.
